subChunks.title: Philosophy & History of Science
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora pulled a battered paperback from the shelf — Karl Popper's The Logic of Scientific Discovery, its spine held together with tape. 'Every scientist thinks they understand how science works,' she said, dropping into her chair. 'They observe, they hypothesise, they test, they conclude. The neat story we tell undergraduates. But philosophers of science have been arguing for seventy years about whether that story is even remotely accurate — and the arguments are not merely academic. They determine what counts as science, which theories get funding, and which claims courts accept as evidence.'

'Popper said science is demarcated from non-science by falsifiability: a claim is scientific only if you can say, in advance, what observation would prove it wrong. Freudian psychoanalysis and Marxist historical theory, he said, were not scientific — they could accommodate any outcome as confirming evidence. That criterion appealed enormously to practising scientists. It was clean, democratic, and devastating to charlatanism.'

She opened the book to a dog-eared page. 'Then Thomas Kuhn came along in 1962 and pointed out that science does not work the way Popper described. Scientists do not abandon a paradigm the moment an anomaly appears. They protect it, surround it with auxiliary hypotheses, and keep working. Revolutions happen only when anomalies accumulate past a breaking point and a new generation is ready to see things differently. Kuhn was describing how science actually works — and the picture was messier, more sociological, more human than anyone liked to admit.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Demarcation Problem

What distinguishes science from non-science — or pseudoscience? This is the demarcation problem, one of philosophy of science's central concerns.

Karl Popper (1902–1994) proposed falsificationism: a statement is scientific if and only if it is falsifiable — there exists a possible observation that would prove it false. 'All swans are white' is falsifiable (produce a black swan); 'God loves everyone in His own way' is not. Popper saw science as a process of conjecture and refutation, with theories never proved true but only surviving attempted falsification. The strength of a theory lies in the boldness of its predictions and its survival of rigorous attempts to disprove it.

Critics of falsificationism note the Duhem-Quine thesis: no scientific hypothesis is tested in isolation. Every test involves auxiliary hypotheses (about instruments, environmental conditions, mathematical models). When a prediction fails, the blame can be shifted to any auxiliary hypothesis rather than the core theory — making strict falsification difficult in practice. Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance was 'falsifying' Newtonian gravity for decades before Einstein resolved it; astronomers postulated an undiscovered planet (Vulcan) to protect Newton's theory rather than abandoning it.

Scientific Revolutions — Thomas Kuhn

Thomas Kuhn (1922–1996) in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) introduced the concept of the paradigm: a shared set of assumptions, methods, standards, and exemplary problem-solutions that define normal science within a discipline. Normal science is puzzle-solving within the paradigm — filling in gaps, refining measurements, extending established theory. Anomalies — observations that resist resolution within the paradigm — are initially set aside or explained away.

When anomalies accumulate and confidence in the paradigm erodes, a scientific revolution occurs: an established paradigm is replaced by a new, incommensurable one. Kuhn argued that paradigm shifts are not simply the result of rational theory-choice but involve sociological factors — generational change, persuasion, community dynamics. Crucially, he introduced incommensurability: competing paradigms often use the same words with different meanings, or solve different problems, making direct rational comparison impossible. Mass means something different in Newtonian and Einsteinian mechanics.

Kuhn's examples: Copernican revolution (geocentric → heliocentric), Lavoisier's oxygen theory (phlogiston → oxidation), the Darwinian revolution, quantum mechanics (classical → quantum). His account was controversial because it seemed to make paradigm choice partly irrational and to undermine scientific objectivity.

Imre Lakatos — Research Programmes

Imre Lakatos (1922–1974) attempted to reconcile Popper and Kuhn with scientific research programmes. A research programme has a hard core — central theoretical commitments protected from falsification by a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that can be modified to accommodate anomalies. Research programmes are progressive if they successfully predict novel facts; they are degenerating if they only make post-hoc accommodations to anomalies without predicting anything new. Scientists are rational to stay with a degenerating programme for a time, but should eventually shift to a progressive competitor.

Lakatos's framework explains why Newton's programme withstood apparent falsifications (Neptune was discovered to explain Mercury; anomalous Uranus orbit predicted Neptune's existence) and why programmes like Ptolemaic astronomy were eventually abandoned. It preserves Popperian rationalism while acknowledging Kuhn's sociological reality.

Paul Feyerabend — Against Method

Paul Feyerabend (1924–1994) in Against Method (1975) argued that no single methodological rule characterises all successful science. Galileo's heliocentric advocacy violated many prevailing methodological norms — he used the telescope (whose reliability was contested), introduced ad hoc hypotheses, and appealed to rhetorical rather than purely evidential arguments. Science progresses through 'anything goes' — pluralism of methods, including borrowing from art, mythology, and politics. Feyerabend was provocative and sometimes inconsistent, but his core point — that scientific methodology is more opportunistic and context-dependent than its official self-description — has been influential in science studies.

Bayesian Epistemology

Bayesian philosophy of science models scientific reasoning through probability. Scientists begin with a prior probability P(H) for a hypothesis, update it to a posterior probability P(H|E) upon evidence E using Bayes' theorem: P(H|E) = P(E|H) × P(H) / P(E). This framework handles graded degrees of belief, explains why novel predictions provide more confirmatory power than accommodated observations, and formalises the role of prior knowledge. Critics raise the problem of priors: two scientists with different priors may never converge, even given identical evidence — especially troubling for extraordinary claims.

History of Science — Key Episodes

The history of science reveals how theories emerge from social, technological, and philosophical contexts. The Scientific Revolution (16th–17th centuries) — Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, Newton — established the mathematical-experimental method and displaced Aristotelian natural philosophy. The Chemical Revolution (Lavoisier, 1770s–80s) introduced quantitative mass conservation and the element concept. Geology's deep time (Hutton, Lyell, 1780s–1830s) provided the temporal scale that Darwin needed. Darwin's natural selection was resisted not merely on religious grounds but because inheritance mechanisms were unknown; only with Mendelian genetics (rediscovered 1900) and the Modern Synthesis (1930s–40s) did natural selection gain full acceptance. Continental drift (Wegener, 1912) was rejected for fifty years before plate tectonics provided a mechanism (paleomagnetism, seafloor spreading, 1950s–60s).

These episodes show that correct theories can be resisted for decades when the supporting technology, community readiness, or mechanistic explanation is absent — and that history of science is indispensable for understanding contemporary controversies.

storyBeats.text: 'Popper's criterion is elegant: a theory is scientific if it is falsifiable. Astrology predicts everything and nothing; it can always explain any birth chart outcome. That is why Popper called it a pseudoscience. Psychoanalysis and Marxism, the same problem — they accommodate every observation as confirming.'

'But the Duhem-Quine thesis is the fly in the ointment. When an experiment contradicts a theory, you never test just the theory — you test the theory plus every auxiliary assumption: the instrument works, the sample is pure, the mathematics is applied correctly. Which link in the chain do you cut?'

'Kuhn said: look at what scientists actually do. They do not abandon paradigms when anomalies appear. They defend them, patch them, work around them. Revolutions come when anomalies pile up and a new generation arrives without loyalty to the old paradigm. Science is deeply sociological.'

'Lakatos tried to save Popper from Kuhn: research programmes, hard cores, protective belts. Progressive programmes predict novel facts; degenerating ones only retrodict. The history of science can be reconstructed as rational — but Lakatos had to allow quite a lot of latitude before the reconstruction worked.'

'Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912. For forty years the geology establishment rejected it — there was no plausible mechanism. In the 1960s, paleomagnetism and seafloor spreading provided the mechanism. Continental drift became plate tectonics overnight. The paradigm had resisted a correct theory for half a century.'

Theodora closed the Popper. 'Philosophy of science matters because it shapes what we fund, what we publish, what courts accept as expert testimony, and which voices get labelled fringe versus mainstream. It is not just academic. It is political.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what Karl Popper meant by falsifiability, and give one example of a scientific claim and one example of a non-scientific claim, explaining why each is or is not falsifiable.
learningObjectives: Explain and critically evaluate Popper's falsificationism, including the Duhem-Quine objection
Describe Kuhn's model of scientific revolutions — normal science, paradigm, anomaly, revolution, incommensurability
Compare Lakatos's research programme framework with Popper and Kuhn, identifying its advantages and limitations
Analyse historical case studies (continental drift, Darwinian evolution) to illustrate how social and contextual factors affect theory acceptance
commonMistakes: Treating falsificationism as the consensus view of science rather than a contested philosophical position with known objections
Confusing Kuhn's incommensurability with the claim that paradigm choice is purely irrational — Kuhn did not deny that evidence matters, only that it is never the sole factor
Applying the label 'pseudoscience' without precision — falsifiability is one demarcation criterion but not the only one (testability, consilience, and predictive success are also relevant)
Treating the history of science as linear progress toward truth rather than as a series of contingent episodes shaped by social and technological context
assessmentCriteria: Accurately articulates the demarcation problem and evaluates at least three philosophical responses (Popper, Kuhn, Lakatos) with their respective strengths and weaknesses
Applies the Duhem-Quine thesis to a concrete scientific case to explain why strict falsification is more complex than it appears
Uses a historical case study to illustrate how non-evidential factors influenced theory acceptance or rejection
Demonstrates understanding of Bayesian confirmation theory and its advantages over purely falsificationist accounts
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Case Study Analysis: Continental Drift and Plate Tectonics

Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, citing the fit of continental coastlines, matching fossils across the Atlantic, and palaeoclimatic evidence (coal in Antarctica). The geological establishment rejected his theory until the 1960s, when seafloor spreading and paleomagnetism provided a mechanism and the theory was reformulated as plate tectonics.

  1. Apply Kuhn's framework: what was the prevailing paradigm in geology before plate tectonics? What anomalies did Wegener identify, and why were they resisted within the existing paradigm?
  2. Apply Lakatos's research programme framework: was the geological establishment's resistance rational or irrational? What constitutes the 'hard core' and 'protective belt' of the pre-plate-tectonics programme?
  3. Apply Popper's criterion: is continental drift theory falsifiable? What observations would falsify modern plate tectonics theory?
  4. Reflect: what does this case suggest about the relationship between evidence, mechanism, and paradigm change in science?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Kuhn's framework: The prevailing paradigm was permanentism — the idea that continents and ocean basins are fixed features of the Earth, potentially rising and falling (geosyncline theory) but not horizontally drifting. Anomalies: Wegener's coastline fit, Glossopteris fossils on multiple southern continents, Mesosaurus fossils on both sides of the Atlantic, Carboniferous glacial deposits in tropical Africa. These were resisted because: (a) they could be explained within the old paradigm via land bridges or coordinated sea-floor sinking, and (b) Wegener proposed a mechanism (centrifugal force) that was physically impossible — geologists correctly rejected the mechanism even when the evidence was suggestive.

2. Lakatos's framework: The resistance was partly rational: Lakatos would say the permanentist programme was not yet clearly degenerating — it still generated research (seismic surveys, sedimentation studies). Wegener's programme was not yet progressive enough (it predicted continental shapes but not novel, independently testable facts). When paleomagnetism revealed seafloor magnetic stripes symmetric about mid-ocean ridges — a novel prediction of plate tectonics — the new programme became clearly progressive. The hard core of permanentism: fixed ocean-continent boundaries. Protective belt: land bridges, vertical movements, sinking isotherms.

3. Popper's criterion: Plate tectonics is highly falsifiable. Specific predictions: GPS measurements should show continental plates moving at specific rates (confirmed: 2–15 cm/year); paleomagnetism should show symmetric reversal patterns on either side of mid-ocean ridges (confirmed); subduction zones should produce specific earthquake depth-distance patterns (Benioff zones) — all confirmed. Falsifiers: continents that do not move, or move in directions inconsistent with the theory.

4. Reflection: The case shows that correct theories can be resisted when they lack a physically plausible mechanism. Evidence alone was insufficient; a mechanism was required before the community accepted the theory. This supports both Kuhn (community inertia and sociological resistance) and Lakatos (waiting for the programme to become clearly progressive) over naive Popperian falsificationism. But it also shows that ultimately evidence was decisive — once paleomagnetism provided an unambiguous and novel prediction, the field shifted rapidly.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: String theory in physics has been a dominant research programme for over forty years, attracting thousands of physicists and producing extensive mathematical developments. It has not yet made a confirmed, novel, empirically testable prediction. Some critics argue it is therefore not science. Write a structured argument (~300 words) that: (a) applies Popper's falsificationism, Kuhn's paradigm concept, and Lakatos's progressive/degenerating distinction to evaluate string theory's scientific status; (b) assesses whether any of these frameworks gives a satisfying answer; and (c) concludes with your own position, defended with philosophical and scientific reasoning.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Framework applications:

Popper: String theory's core predictions (extra dimensions, supersymmetric partners, new particles) are in principle falsifiable — particle accelerators could detect superpartners; extra dimensions would affect gravity at small scales. However, the energy scales required (Planck scale, ~10¹⁹ GeV) are far beyond any foreseeable accelerator. In practice, string theory has not been falsified, but neither has it been testable in any near-term sense. Popper's criterion is formally satisfied but practically hollow.

Kuhn: String theory resembles Kuhn's 'normal science' within a post-Standard Model paradigm — puzzle-solving, mathematical elaboration, and community consolidation around a shared research programme. The community has invested decades in string theory; alternative approaches (loop quantum gravity, causal set theory) remain minority programmes. Whether string theory is a paradigm undergoing normal science or a pre-paradigm field without consensus is contested.

Lakatos: The critical question is whether string theory is progressive or degenerating. It has generated novel mathematical results (AdS/CFT correspondence, which has found applications in condensed matter physics and nuclear physics). These are novel predictions, but within mathematics/physics duality rather than direct empirical tests. By Lakatos, a programme that generates novel results — even mathematical ones — is not obviously degenerating. But the failure to make confirmed, independently testable, empirical predictions for forty years is concerning.

(b) Assessment: None of the frameworks gives a fully satisfying answer. Popper's formal falsifiability is too weak (any claim about unobservable entities is 'in principle' falsifiable). Kuhn's is descriptive, not normative. Lakatos is closest — the progressive/degenerating distinction tracks something real — but defining 'novel' broadly enough to include mathematical results risks making the criterion toothless.

(c) Position: String theory occupies a legitimate but epistemically liminal space: it is rigorous mathematical physics, generates genuine insights, and makes conditional empirical predictions. Labelling it 'not science' is philosophically crude. A better description: it is an empirically underdetermined research programme of high theoretical fecundity but currently untestable core claims. Science funding and community should continue to support multiple competing approaches — loop quantum gravity, causal dynamical triangulations — rather than concentrating resources on a single unfalsified programme.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The philosophical claim that any hypothesis is only tested together with a set of auxiliary assumptions, making it impossible to blame a single hypothesis when a prediction fails.
Kuhn's claim that successive paradigms are incompatible in ways that prevent direct rational comparison — shared terms may have different meanings across paradigms.
A formal model of scientific reasoning in which evidence updates degrees of belief using Bayes' theorem, allowing quantitative treatment of hypothesis confirmation.
Hume's challenge: no number of observed instances logically entails a general law; we cannot prove the future will resemble the past, making all empirical generalisations uncertain.
The thesis that evidence is logically compatible with multiple, mutually inconsistent theories — evidence alone cannot uniquely determine which theory is correct.
The study of how scientific knowledge is produced by communities, including the roles of peer review, funding structures, authority, and social identity in shaping scientific consensus.

options: Puzzle-solving within an accepted paradigm, without questioning its fundamental assumptions
The process of testing and falsifying hypotheses by designing experiments
The rational comparison of competing theories using Bayesian probability
The period following a scientific revolution when a new paradigm becomes established
questions.correctAnswer: Puzzle-solving within an accepted paradigm, without questioning its fundamental assumptions
questions.explanationHtml: For Kuhn, normal science is the day-to-day activity of scientists working within an accepted paradigm — solving puzzles, refining measurements, extending theory — without challenging the paradigm's core assumptions. Paradigm-challenging activity is rare and constitutes revolutionary science, not normal science.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher claims that homeopathy is effective because every patient who received it in their study either improved or was explained as 'not responding due to underlying stress'. Which philosophical concept does this illustrate?
options: Unfalsifiability — the claim can accommodate any outcome as confirming evidence
The Duhem-Quine thesis — auxiliary hypotheses are being used to protect the core claim
Incommensurability — homeopathy and conventional medicine use different conceptual frameworks
A degenerating research programme — the programme makes no novel predictions
questions.correctAnswer: Unfalsifiability — the claim can accommodate any outcome as confirming evidence
questions.explanationHtml: Popper's falsificationism identifies this as the hallmark of a non-scientific claim: any possible outcome (improvement, or 'not responding due to stress') is interpreted as confirming the hypothesis. There is no specified observation that would count as evidence against it. While the Duhem-Quine thesis is also partially applicable, the primary issue is straightforward unfalsifiability.

questions.questionHtml: Lakatos argues that research programmes are 'degenerating' rather than 'progressive'. What is the most precise meaning of this distinction?
options: A progressive programme predicts novel facts that are subsequently confirmed; a degenerating one only accommodates known anomalies post hoc
A progressive programme uses mathematical formalism; a degenerating one relies on qualitative description
A progressive programme has more researchers than a degenerating one
A degenerating programme has been formally falsified, while a progressive one has not
questions.correctAnswer: A progressive programme predicts novel facts that are subsequently confirmed; a degenerating one only accommodates known anomalies post hoc
questions.explanationHtml: Lakatos's key criterion is predictive novelty: a programme is empirically progressive if it predicts hitherto unobserved facts, some of which are confirmed. A degenerating programme only adjusts its protective belt to explain known anomalies without predicting anything genuinely new. This is not about researcher numbers, mathematical formalism, or formal falsification — a programme can be both unfalsified and degenerating if it is merely reactive rather than predictive.
